title: Bread and Beer
objective: After this level you can describe what Egyptians ate and drank.
summary: Bread and beer, both made from grain, were Egypt’s staples. Beer was thick and nourishing, food rations served as pay, and sandy bread wore down people’s teeth.

cards.headline: Ask an ancient Egyptian what’s for dinner. Bread. And beer.
cards.body: Every day. Bread and beer were the staples of the Egyptian diet, and both came from the same grain. Here’s why beer counted as food, and why bread came with a price.

cards.headline: Same grain, two jobs
cards.body: Remember the emmer wheat and barley from Level 4? That grain became bread and beer, the staples of the diet. Bread was made mainly with emmer, baked as flat loaves a bit like pita or as tall cones. Beer used basically the same ingredients, so baking and brewing went hand in hand. The farming year ended at the dinner table.

cards.headline: Beer was a meal
cards.body: Forget a crisp lager. Egyptian beer was thick and cloudy, probably weaker than modern beer, and an important source of nutrition rather than just a treat. And since Egypt didn’t use coins or paper money, food doubled as pay: workers and household staff were often paid in rations. Payday smelled like a bakery.

cards.headline: A bakery in miniature
cards.body: Remember Meketre, whose model boat you met in Level 5? His tomb also held a model bakery and brewery, made about 1981 to 1975 BCE and now at the Met. Tiny men crush grain with pestles, women grind it into flour, and a basket of cone-shaped loaves waits in the middle. Bread and beer shared one workshop because they shared one set of ingredients.

cards.headline: The gritty truth
cards.body: That flour came with extras. Heavy tooth wear is the most common dental problem found in ancient Egyptian remains, and experts blame a coarse diet made even rougher by sand, mostly blown in on the wind, that ended up in the bread. Every loaf was a little bit of sandpaper. Egypt’s favorite food slowly ate Egypt’s teeth.

mascot.line: Imagine a little sand in every bite, every day, for life. Your teeth would notice too.

cards.headline: Bread and beer: served
learned: Bread and beer were the daily staples
Both came from the same grain, mainly emmer for bread
Beer was thick, nourishing food; wages came as rations
Sandy bread wore down Egyptians’ teeth

questions.prompt: What were the two staples of the ancient Egyptian diet?

options.label: Rice and wine
options.rationale: Egyptians lived mainly on grain made into bread and beer.

options.label: Fish and milk
options.rationale: These were eaten, but they weren’t the staples.

options.label: Dates and honey
options.rationale: Sweet extras, not the daily base.

questions.explanation: Bread and beer, both made from grain, were eaten and drunk every day.

questions.prompt: Why were ancient Egyptians’ teeth so often badly worn down?

options.label: They chewed raw sugar cane all day
options.rationale: The culprit was in their bread.

options.label: Sand and grit got into their bread
They cleaned their teeth with stones
options.rationale: The wear came from what they ate.

options.label: Their beer was strongly acidic
options.rationale: Experts blame a coarse, sandy diet.

questions.explanation: Sand, mostly wind-blown, got into the bread and ground teeth down over a lifetime.

questions.prompt: From Level 4: Egyptian bread was made mainly from which of Egypt’s main crops?

options.label: Flax
options.rationale: Flax was woven into linen, not baked.

options.label: Lentils
options.rationale: Lentils were a crop, but bread was mainly emmer.

options.label: Onions
options.rationale: Onions grew alongside, but bread was grain.

questions.explanation: Bread was made mainly with emmer wheat, one of the main crops grown in the flood’s silt.
